catalog_quote: 2.5.1 Stress. The documentation of the language as per LE/T in particular, which includes stress marks in nearly every word, clearly demonstrates first syllable stress. This is supported also by evidence from related languages (H/Nu, Amery 2000). The stress on a few words has shifted in present usage, including the highly salient Nhaˈrangga ‘Narungga’ itself. While the stress on this word in particular is unlikely to shift backwards in the broader Narungga community, its nonconformity with the general pattern of the language has drawn comments from those most closely involved in the language renewal. Some place names which have been transferred into English have also undergone a stress shift. new_statements.quote: The documentation of the language as per LE/T in particular, which includes stress marks in nearly every word, clearly demonstrates first syllable stress. This is supported also by evidence from related languages (H/Nu, Amery 2000). The stress on a few words has shifted in present usage, including the highly salient Nhaˈrangga 'Narungga' itself. [...] Some place names which have been transferred into English have also undergone a stress shift. There is some indication of shifting stress in longer words with affixes added, such as banggaˈrangga (banggara-ngga country-LOC). Other than these few exceptions, first-syllable stress is taught without controversy (although not necessarily always adopted easily by speaker/learners).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word. Eira bases this on the historical record (Tindale's 1930s notes, which mark stress on nearly every word) and on the sister Thura-Yura languages Nukunu and Kaurna; it is the rule taught in the renewed language. Black's first-hand 1919 transcriptions (p.80) independently state that the great majority of words are accented on the first syllable, with a slight secondary stress on the third syllable of four-syllable words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Eira 2010 gives no general rule; fn. 27 (p.81) notes Tindale's placement of secondary stress in the reduplicated bagaggu (< /bagu+bagu/). Black 1920 p.80: in four-syllable words 'a slight secondary stress on the third syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: Eira 2010 p.39: present-day second-syllable stress on the name Nhaˈrangga itself, on some place names taken into English, and some tendency to shift stress in longer affixed words (banggaˈrangga); fn. 2 p.54 flags Tindale's <a'pulu> 'wattle grub' as an unusual non-initial marking. Black 1920 pp.85-88 marks second-syllable accent on bin'dirja, mailku'wata, mara'wati and says (p.80) he cannot explain such cases.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule; Narungga is a reclaimed (renewal) language with no fluent L1 speakers since the 20th century, so Eira's phonology (§2.1) describes the target/teaching phonology of the renewed language justified from historical transcriptions (chiefly Tindale 1936 and MS notes, Black 1920, Johnson 1930-31) and sister languages. Black 1920 is the only phonetically trained first-hand record of L1 speakers (Sarah Newchurch, Harry Richards, 1919) and its p.80 stress remark is phrased for all four vocabularies in the paper.
new_statements.identity_note: Narungga (naru1238, ISO nnr), Yorke Peninsula, Thura-Yura subgroup of Pama-Nyungan. Eira 2010 describes the renewed (reclaimed) language of the NAPA project, with the stress rule justified from historical transcriptions (Tindale 1936, Black 1920) and sister languages Nukunu and Kaurna; Black 1920 records the Narrunga of Point Pearce L1 speakers in 1919. No dialect split is at issue.
